imageCaption: A corner bodega with handwritten signs in the window. The selection of flowers suddenly triples, then returns to normal. A neighborhood shifting to meet a family halfway.
text:
The flower situation at the bodega was objectively impossible.

This was the conclusion Aaliyah reached approximately thirty seconds after Marco called her to report that Mrs. Chen, who owned the corner store where the family had become accidental regulars, was now selling flowers.

Specifically, she was selling seventeen different varieties of flowers. In a bodega that had previously devoted its entire floral inventory to a single wire display of sad carnations in a bucket.

"She says they just appeared," Marco reported over the phone. He was standing inside the bodega, apparently because he had reflexively started documenting things that didn't make sense. "She opened up this morning, unlocked the back cooler, and there were roses. Then orchids. Then those ones that look like they're trying to be both a flower and a firework at the same time."

"Bird of paradise," Aaliyah said automatically. She was already moving toward the door. "I'm coming."

"Also," Marco added, "she wants to know if you want them specifically because she's reserved the good ones and she's refusing to sell them until you arrive. Which is customer service excellence or witchcraft. I haven't decided which."

Aaliyah arrived at the bodega to find that Marco had been underselling the situation. The entire front window had been reorganized into a greenhouse. Sunflowers. Dahlias. Something that looked like a crown made of purple velvet. Lilies in every imaginable color. And the flowers were arranged so specifically, so deliberately, that it looked less like a random delivery and more like an answer to a question nobody had asked yet.

Mrs. Chen was standing behind the counter with the expression of a woman who'd been running a bodega for thirty years and had thought she understood her inventory. She'd clearly been wrong.

"They weren't here yesterday," she said immediately. She was holding a receipt book like she wanted to convince Aaliyah that she was still operating in the realm of things that made sense. "I lock up at nine. I come in at five AM. I check the cooler. Everything is normal. By six AM, I have flowers like I'm running a botanical garden."

"Did you check the back door?" Aaliyah asked. She was already pulling out her phone. "Are there boxes? Delivery records?"

"Nothing," Mrs. Chen said. She gestured at the flowers like they'd just announced they were running for mayor. "They're just... here. And they're perfect. Every single one is perfect, which is not how flowers work. Flowers are supposed to wilt. Flowers are supposed to have bad petals. These flowers look like they're defying entropy."

This was accurate. Aaliyah could see it immediately. The flowers didn't look like they'd been picked and arranged. They looked like they'd been grown specifically to exist in this moment, to look exactly this perfect, to make the bodega look like someone had decided that a corner store could be the most beautiful place in the neighborhood.

"Are they for the sancocho?" Marco asked. He was taking photos of the arrangements with the intensity of someone documenting something that mattered. "Is the timeline just... helping?"

"Why would the timeline care about flowers?" Aaliyah said.

"Because you're cooking for fourteen addresses tomorrow," Luisana said. She appeared in the bodega doorway with the timing of someone who'd been tracking her daughter and had apparently developed a sense for when situations required parental presence. "Because you're feeding a neighborhood. Because a neighborhood that knows it's being seen shows up in small ways. The timeline isn't giving you flowers, sweetheart. Your neighborhood is."

Mrs. Chen looked at Luisana like she'd just explained something crucial. "Your daughter is feeding people on my street?"

"Tomorrow," Aaliyah said. "Second Sunday. Fourteen addresses. And apparently the bodega is going to provide color."

"I'm going to do more than provide color," Mrs. Chen said. She was already moving toward the flowers, already reaching for the dahlias and the purple crown thing. "What flowers work with soup? What goes on a table with food that doesn't make the food look like it's competing?"

"Greenery," Luisana said. She was already studying the arrangement like a journalist preparing to document the answer to something she'd been wondering about. "Long stems. Things that frame the food instead of fighting it. What about those?" She pointed at delicate fern-like flowers in shades of white and cream.

Mrs. Chen's entire body shifted. She went from confused to purposeful to absolutely certain that she was now a co-creator in something important. "You're right," she said. "Frame, don't fight. And the white ones. The ones that are just barely anything. Those should go in the middle so the sancocho is the star."

"That's exactly right," Aaliyah said.

And then she realized: this was how the neighborhood worked. This was how a community that had never planned anything together suddenly knew exactly how to help.

Mrs. Chen started preparing bundles of flowers with the precision of someone who'd just discovered her secondary calling. Marco kept documenting because Marco documented things. Luisana was writing in her journal, capturing Mrs. Chen's insights, building the narrative of how a bodega became part of a feeding.

"How many tables?" Mrs. Chen asked.

"Fourteen addresses means we'll set up at five locations," Aaliyah said. She was still calculating, still building the logistics in her head. "Two houses with indoor space, three with porches or small yards. Three centerpieces per location, so forty-two flowers total?"

"I'll do fifty," Mrs. Chen said. "Extra. For your house. So you remember which table was the beginning."

The flowers suddenly made sense. Not as random glitch appearance—though they might be that too—but as Mrs. Chen insisting that the Gomez family's work mattered. As a bodega owner saying: I see what you're building. Let me hold some of the beauty.

"Thank you," Aaliyah said. And she meant it. She meant it the way you mean things when you suddenly understand that your family didn't move to New York alone. They moved here and built resonance, and the resonance built itself back, and a neighborhood became conscious of what it wanted to be.

Sully appeared in the bodega doorway with a piece of carrot and the expression of a dog who'd been tracking his family and had opinions about flowers. He barked approval at Mrs. Chen, which apparently meant she was now certified as part of the official support system.

"I'll have them ready tomorrow morning," Mrs. Chen said. She was already thinking about water, about delivery, about the logistics of making sure flowers survived their journey from bodega to neighborhood table. "What time do you start?"

"Eleven AM," Aaliyah said.

"I'll have them here at ten-thirty," Mrs. Chen said. "And I'm sending my daughter with them because she should see this. She should know what a neighborhood looks like when it decides to help."

Aaliyah left the bodega with Marco and Luisana, her phone full of flower photos, her mind spinning with the logistics of Sunday, her heart very full with the specific knowledge that they weren't doing this alone.

The timeline had sent flowers.

But the neighborhood had sent choice. Effort. The deliberate decision to be part of something beautiful.

And somehow, that mattered more.

"Tomorrow," Luisana said as they walked back toward the apartment. "Tomorrow you feed fourteen addresses and prove that a neighborhood isn't just a collection of addresses. It's a collection of people who are waiting for permission to care about the same thing."

"What if we fail?" Aaliyah asked.

"Then the bodega owner will have very nice flowers to mark the occasion," Luisana said. "Failure is just a different version of success. Ask your father. He's made an entire life out of proving that."

Tomorrow would tell the story.

But tonight, the neighborhood already knew how to help.
